claim: Substance P and CGRPα are expressed at high levels in pain-responsive neurons from the periphery to the brain.
source: Both peptides and their receptors are expressed at high levels in pain-responsive neurons from the periphery to the brain making them attractive therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data presented.

claim: Drugs targeting Substance P and CGRPα pathways individually did not relieve pain in clinical trials.
source: However, drugs targeting these pathways individually did not relieve pain in clinical trials.
evidence: This statement references clinical trial outcomes, which are cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are extensively co-expressed.
source: Since Substance P and CGRPα are extensively co-expressed, we hypothesized that their simultaneous inhibition would be required for effective analgesia.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα peptides were undetectable throughout the nervous system of DKO mice.
source: As expected, Substance P and CGRPα peptides were undetectable throughout the nervous system of DKO mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: DKO mice displayed largely intact responses to mechanical, thermal, chemical, and visceral pain stimuli, as well as itch.
source: To our surprise, these animals displayed largely intact responses to mechanical, thermal, chemical, and visceral pain stimuli, as well as itch.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Chronic inflammatory pain was unaffected by loss of Substance P and CGRPα.
source: Moreover, chronic inflammatory pain and neurogenic inflammation were unaffected by loss of the two peptides.
evidence: This is supported by CFA and PGE2 data in Figure 3.

claim: Neurogenic inflammation was unaffected by loss of Substance P and CGRPα.
source: Moreover, chronic inflammatory pain and neurogenic inflammation were unaffected by loss of the two peptides.
evidence: This is supported by Evans blue extravasation and edema measurements in Figure 3E-J.

claim: Neuropathic pain evoked by nerve injury was preserved in peptide-deficient mice.
source: Finally, neuropathic pain evoked by nerve injury or chemotherapy treatment was also preserved in peptide-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by spared nerve injury data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Neuropathic pain evoked by chemotherapy treatment was preserved in peptide-deficient mice.
source: Finally, neuropathic pain evoked by nerve injury or chemotherapy treatment was also preserved in peptide-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by oxaliplatin data in Figure 4D.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are not required for the transmission of acute and chronic pain.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that even in combination, Substance P and CGRPα are not required for the transmission of acute and chronic pain.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive behavioral data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Substance P is an 11-amino acid peptide first discovered as a tissue extract with contractile activity.
source: Substance P is an 11-amino acid peptide first discovered as a tissue extract with contractile activity (V Euler and Gaddum, 1931).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CGRPα is a 37-amino acid peptide and potent vasodilator identified as the alternatively spliced product of the calcitonin gene.
source: CGRPα is a 37-amino acid peptide and potent vasodilator identified as the alternatively spliced product of the calcitonin gene (Amara et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both Substance P and CGRPα are highly expressed in pain-responsive neurons throughout the nervous system.
source: Both Substance P and CGRPα are highly expressed in pain-responsive neurons throughout the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Strong activation of nociceptor sensory neurons causes peptide secretion and neurogenic inflammation.
source: In the periphery, strong activation of nociceptor sensory neurons is reported to cause peptide secretion and neurogenic inflammation (Chiu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Release of Substance P and CGRPα in the spinal cord and brainstem may alter pain transmission in ascending pain pathways.
source: Similarly, release of Substance P and CGRPα in the spinal cord and brainstem may alter pain transmission in ascending pain pathways (Huang et al., 2019; Latremoliere and Woolf, 2009; Löken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are prominently enriched in brain areas known to be involved in pain, including the periaqueductal grey, parabrachial nucleus and amygdala.
source: In the brain, these molecules are prominently enriched in areas known to be involved in pain, including the periaqueductal grey, parabrachial nucleus and amygdala (Barik et al., 2018; Lein et al., 2007; Palmiter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Selective antagonists of the Substance P receptor NKR1 failed to relieve chronic pain in human clinical trials.
source: However, selective antagonists of the Substance P receptor NKR1 failed to relieve chronic pain in human clinical trials (Hill, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical trial review.

claim: CGRP monoclonal antibodies and receptor blockers have proven effective for subsets of migraine patients.
source: Although CGRP monoclonal antibodies and receptor blockers have proven effective for subsets of migraine patients, their usefulness for other types of pain in humans is unclear (De Matteis et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Knockout mice deficient in Substance P, CGRPα or their receptors have been reported to display some pain deficits, but the analgesic effects are neither large nor consistent between studies.
source: In line with this, knockout mice deficient in Substance P, CGRPα or their receptors have been reported to display some pain deficits, but the analgesic effects are neither large nor consistent between studies (Cao et al., 1998; De Felipe et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2012; Salmon et al., 2001; Salmon et al., 1999; Zimmer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Ablating or inhibiting peptidergic nociceptors causes profound decreases in heat sensitivity, inflammatory heat hyperalgesia, and some forms of mechanical allodynia.
source: By contrast, ablating or inhibiting peptidergic nociceptors causes profound decreases in heat sensitivity, inflammatory heat hyperalgesia, and some forms of mechanical allodynia (Cowie et al., 2018; McCoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice with silenced Substance P or CGRPα-expressing neurons in brain areas such as the parabrachial nucleus show impaired pain behavior.
source: Mice with silenced Substance P or CGRPα-expressing neurons in brain areas such as the parabrachial nucleus also show impaired pain behavior (Barik et al., 2018; Han et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the periphery, Substance P and CGRPα are expressed by largely the same nociceptors, in mice and in humans.
source: In the periphery, Substance P and CGRPα are expressed by largely the same nociceptors, in mice and in humans (Nguyen et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are co-expressed in the brain.
source: The two peptides are also co-expressed in the brain (Pauli et al., 2022; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Redundancy is built into pain pathways because of their importance for survival.
source: Redundancy is built into pain pathways because of their importance for survival and may explain why attenuating the signaling of a single peptide does not recapitulate the analgesic effect of silencing the cell secreting it (Vandewauw et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Naked mole rats release glutamate but not Substance P or CGRPα from nociceptors and show striking absence of inflammatory pain.
source: We predicted these DKO animals might recapitulate the striking absence of inflammatory pain observed in naked mole rats that release glutamate but not Substance P or CGRPα from nociceptors (Park et al., 2008; Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on naked mole rats.

claim: A homozygous Tac1-RFP knockin-knockout line was used to remove the Tac1 gene encoding preprotachykinin, the precursor for Substance P and Neurokinin A.
source: A homozygous Tac1-RFP knockin-knockout line was used to remove the Tac1 gene encoding preprotachykinin, the precursor for Substance P and Neurokinin A (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the genetic approach used, supported by a citation.

claim: No detectable Substance P immunostaining was observed in pain-relevant areas including the dorsal root ganglion, dorsal horn of the spinal cord, parabrachial nucleus and periaqueductal gray in DKO mice.
source: As expected, no detectable Substance P immunostaining was observed in pain-relevant areas including the dorsal root ganglion, dorsal horn of the spinal cord, parabrachial nucleus and periaqueductal gray (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A Calca-Cre mouse at homozygosity is a knockout for the Calca gene encoding the Calcitonin and CGRPα peptides.
source: To eliminate CGRPα signaling, we used a Calca-Cre mouse, which at homozygosity is a knockout for the Calca gene encoding the Calcitonin and CGRPα peptides (Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the genetic approach used, supported by citations.

claim: CGRP immunoreactivity was undetectable in DRG, spinal cord and the amygdala of DKO mice.
source: We were unable to detect CGRP immunoreactivity in DRG, spinal cord and the amygdala (Figure 1B) validating the DKO approach.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Capsaicin-evoked secretion from WT DRG neurons activates Substance P-sniffer cells.
source: Control DRGs treated with capsaicin evoked robust GCaMP responses in surrounding Substance P-sniffer cells (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Capsaicin-stimulated DKO-DRG neurons induced no Substance P-sniffer cell responses.
source: In contrast, capsaicin stimulated DKO-DRG neurons induced no Substance P-sniffer cell responses (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: WT DRG neurons cultured with CGRP-sniffer cells showed strong increases in calcium consistent with CGRP receptor activity in response to capsaicin application.
source: When we cultured WT DRG neurons with the CGRP-sniffer cells, we observed strong increases in calcium consistent with CGRP receptor activity in response to capsaicin application (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: DKO neurons evoked markedly reduced activity in adjacent CGRP-sniffer cells.
source: However, DKO neurons evoked markedly reduced activity in the adjacent sniffer cells (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F-H (note: the text reference appears to be an error, should be 1F-H).

claim: Deletion of Tac1 and Calca completely blocks the endogenous activation of Substance P and CGRP receptors by nociceptor neurons.
source: In combination, these experiments demonstrate that deletion of Tac1 and Calca completely blocks the endogenous activation of Substance P and CGRP receptors by nociceptor neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the sniffer cell imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Responses to mechanical stimulation by von Frey hairs were quantitatively indistinguishable between DKO and WT mice.
source: Specifically, responses to mechanical stimulation by von Frey hairs, pinpricks or an alligator clip were quantitatively indistinguishable (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Responses to mechanical stimulation by pinpricks were quantitatively indistinguishable between DKO and WT mice.
source: Specifically, responses to mechanical stimulation by von Frey hairs, pinpricks or an alligator clip were quantitatively indistinguishable (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Responses to mechanical stimulation by an alligator clip were quantitatively indistinguishable between DKO and WT mice.
source: Specifically, responses to mechanical stimulation by von Frey hairs, pinpricks or an alligator clip were quantitatively indistinguishable (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Withdrawal responses to radiant heat stimulation (Hargreaves') were unaffected in DKO mice.
source: In addition, withdrawal responses to radiant heat stimulation (Hargreaves', Figure 2D), and to two noxious Hot Plate temperatures were unaffected in DKO mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Withdrawal responses to two noxious Hot Plate temperatures were unaffected in DKO mice.
source: In addition, withdrawal responses to radiant heat stimulation (Hargreaves', Figure 2D), and to two noxious Hot Plate temperatures were unaffected in DKO mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Responses to cold evoked by acetone were the same between DKO and WT groups.
source: Responses to cold evoked by acetone and dry ice were also the same between groups (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Responses to cold evoked by dry ice were the same between DKO and WT groups.
source: Responses to cold evoked by acetone and dry ice were also the same between groups (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No differences in dorsal horn Fos expression were observed between DKO and WT mice following capsaicin injection.
source: No differences in dorsal horn Fos expression were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Intraplantar injection of AITC evoked similar licking behavior to capsaicin that was unaffected by peptide deletion.
source: Furthermore, intraplantar injection of a different algogen (the Trpa1 agonist allyl isothiocyanate, AITC) evoked similar licking behavior to capsaicin that was unaffected by peptide deletion (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Loss of Substance P and CGRPα does not alter acute withdrawal or coping-like responses to multiple modalities of damaging stimuli applied to the paw.
source: Together these data suggest that loss of the two neuropeptides does not alter acute withdrawal or coping-like responses to multiple modalities of damaging stimuli applied to the paw.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: WT and DKO mice with intraplantar injection of CFA developed strong heat hypersensitivity.
source: Surprisingly, WT and DKO mice with intraplantar injection of CFA developed strong heat hypersensitivity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CFA-induced mechanical hypersensitivity was unaffected by peptide loss.
source: Mechanical hypersensitivity was also unaffected by peptide loss (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PGE2 injection elicited short-lasting heat hypersensitivity to a similar extent in both WT and DKO mice.
source: PGE2 injection elicited short-lasting heat and mechanical hypersensitivity to a similar extent in both WT and DKO mice (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PGE2 injection elicited short-lasting mechanical hypersensitivity to a similar extent in both WT and DKO mice.
source: PGE2 injection elicited short-lasting heat and mechanical hypersensitivity to a similar extent in both WT and DKO mice (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are not required for the behavioral sensitization associated with both acute and chronic inflammation.
source: Together, these data indicate that Substance P and CGRPα are not required for the behavioral sensitization associated with both acute and chronic inflammation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the CFA and PGE2 data in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Injection of CFA provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed that injection of the inflammatory mediators CFA and PGE2, as well as the algogens AITC and capsaicin, provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: Injection of PGE2 provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed that injection of the inflammatory mediators CFA and PGE2, as well as the algogens AITC and capsaicin, provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: Injection of AITC provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed that injection of the inflammatory mediators CFA and PGE2, as well as the algogens AITC and capsaicin, provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: Injection of capsaicin provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed that injection of the inflammatory mediators CFA and PGE2, as well as the algogens AITC and capsaicin, provoked swelling of the hindpaw of DKO mice to a similar extent as WT mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: No appreciable differences in capsaicin-induced swelling were observed between WT and DKO mice.
source: To examine the development of neurogenic inflammation more rigorously, we measured paw volumes after capsaicin injection, and observed no appreciable differences in capsaicin-induced swelling between WT and DKO mice. (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is supported by paw volume measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Plasma extravasation was intact in DKO mice following capsaicin injection.
source: In addition, using the Evans blue dye method, we found that plasma extravasation was intact in DKO mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by Evans blue measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: AITC-induced edema was similar between WT and DKO mice.
source: Similar results were observed following AITC injection (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by paw volume measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: AITC-induced plasma extravasation was similar between WT and DKO mice.
source: Similar results were observed following AITC injection (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by Evans blue measurements shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are dispensable for some forms of neurogenic inflammation.
source: Therefore, Substance P and CGRPα are dispensable for some forms of neurogenic inflammation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the neurogenic inflammation data in Figure 3E-J.

claim: Static mechanical allodynia evoked by von Frey filaments after spared nerve injury developed to the same degree in DKO mice as in WT mice.
source: First, we performed a sciatic spared nerve injury on DKO animals and found that the static mechanical allodynia evoked by von Frey filaments developed to the same degree as in WT mice, persisting for 3 weeks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Brush-evoked Fos activity in the superficial laminae of the dorsal horn of SNI-treated mice was comparable between genotypes.
source: Brush-evoked Fos activity in the superficial laminae of the dorsal horn of SNI-treated mice – a correlate of dynamic allodynia – was also comparable between genotypes (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: One day after intraplantar oxaliplatin treatment, both DKO and WT animals displayed pronounced pain-like behaviors when placed on a Cold Plate held at 10 °C.
source: One day after intraplantar oxaliplatin treatment, both DKO and WT animals displayed pronounced pain-like behaviors when placed on a Cold Plate held at 10 °C (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are not essential for mechanical or cold allodynia.
source: Substance P and CGRPα are therefore not essential for mechanical or cold allodynia.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the neuropathic pain data in Figure 4.

claim: Both Substance P and CGRPα were dispensable for pain across a wide range of assays.
source: Remarkably, both peptides were dispensable for pain across a wide range of assays.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the behavioral data presented.

claim: Substance P and CGRPα are highly expressed throughout ascending pain pathways and are often found together in the same cells.
source: It is difficult to reconcile our findings with the fact that Substance P and CGRPα are highly expressed throughout ascending pain pathways and are often found together in the same cells. (Pauli et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2020; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Studies of Tac1 and Calca single KO mice reported significant impairments in acute pain, including heat sensitivity, visceral pain and the formalin test.
source: Studies of Tac1 and Calca single KO mice reported significant impairments in acute pain, including heat sensitivity, visceral pain and the formalin test (Cao et al., 1998; Salmon et al., 2001; Salmon et al., 1999; Zimmer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The deficits in single KO mice were modest and inconsistent between studies.
source: Notably, these deficits were modest, and in fact inconsistent between studies (Woolf et al., 1998; Zajdel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ablating either peripheral or central neurons expressing Substance P and CGRPα produces profound analgesia.
source: Nonetheless, ablating either peripheral or central neurons expressing Substance P and CGRPα produces profound analgesia (Barik et al., 2018; Cowie et al., 2018; Han et al., 2015; McCoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons expressing Substance P and CGRPα are all glutamatergic and are thought to co-release neuropeptides to modulate synaptic transmission and neuronal firing.
source: Importantly, these neurons are all glutamatergic and are thought to co-release neuropeptides to modulate synaptic transmission and neuronal firing (Pagani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Primary afferent-derived glutamate is the critical transmitter for most pain sensations.
source: Our work thus substantiates previous findings that established primary afferent-derived glutamate as the critical transmitter for most pain sensations (Lagerström et al., 2010; Lagerström et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2010; Rogoz et al., 2012; Scherrer et al., 2010), and suggests that the two peptides play at most a minor role.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and inferred from the current data.

claim: The two peptides (Substance P and CGRPα) play at most a minor role in pain transmission.
source: Our work thus substantiates previous findings that established primary afferent-derived glutamate as the critical transmitter for most pain sensations (Lagerström et al., 2010; Lagerström et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2010; Rogoz et al., 2012; Scherrer et al., 2010), and suggests that the two peptides play at most a minor role.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive behavioral data showing intact pain responses in DKO mice.

claim: Classical studies show Substance P infusion into the spinal cord elicits pain.
source: Indeed, classical studies show Substance P infusion into the spinal cord elicits pain, but paradoxically in the brain is analgesic (Hylden and Wilcox, 1981; Malick and Goldstein, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Substance P infusion into the brain is analgesic.
source: Indeed, classical studies show Substance P infusion into the spinal cord elicits pain, but paradoxically in the brain is analgesic (Hylden and Wilcox, 1981; Malick and Goldstein, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Knockout of a gene remains the strongest test of whether the molecule it encodes is essential for a biological phenomenon.
source: Despite this, knockout of a gene remains the strongest test of whether the molecule it encodes is essential for a biological phenomenon (Caterina et al., 2000; Chesler et al., 2016; Mishra and Hoon, 2013), and our results clearly demonstrate that Substance P and CGRPα are not required for pain transmission.
evidence: This is a methodological principle supported by citations.

claim: Accumulating evidence indicates that the secretion of Substance P and CGRPα from nociceptor peripheral terminals modulates immune cells and the vasculature in diverse tissues.
source: Rather than directly acting as pain transmitters in the CNS, accumulating evidence indicates that the secretion of these neuropeptides from nociceptor peripheral terminals modulates immune cells and the vasculature in diverse tissues (Chiu et al., 2013; Chiu et al., 2012; Cohen et al., 2019; Lai et al., 2020; Perner et al., 2020; Pinho-Ribeiro et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The development of effective migraine therapeutics targeting CGRPα or its receptor confirm the important role this peptide plays in headache.
source: For example, the development of effective migraine therapeutics targeting CGRPα or its receptor confirm the important role this peptide plays in headache (De Matteis et al., 2020; Tso and Goadsby, 2017), and new efferent functions for both CGRPα and Substance P are regularly being uncovered (Brain, 1997; Caceres et al., 2009; Perner et al., 2020; Pinho-Ribeiro et al., 2016; Wilhelms et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and research studies.

claim: New efferent functions for both CGRPα and Substance P are regularly being uncovered.
source: For example, the development of effective migraine therapeutics targeting CGRPα or its receptor confirm the important role this peptide plays in headache (De Matteis et al., 2020; Tso and Goadsby, 2017), and new efferent functions for both CGRPα and Substance P are regularly being uncovered (Brain, 1997; Caceres et al., 2009; Perner et al., 2020; Pinho-Ribeiro et al., 2016; Wilhelms et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research studies.

claim: Pain-responsive neurons express a rich repertoire of potential signaling molecules, including other neuropeptides.
source: Beyond Substance P and CGRPα, pain-responsive neurons express a rich repertoire of potential signaling molecules, including other neuropeptides.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about pain neurons.

claim: DKO mice were generated by crossing B6.Cg-Calcatm1.1(cre/EGFP)Rpa/J with Tac1-tagRFP-2A-TVA.
source: DKO mice were generated by crossing B6.Cg-Calcatm1.1(cre/EGFP)Rpa/J (Jax #033168) with Tac1-tagRFP-2A-TVA (Carter et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the breeding strategy used to generate the experimental animals.

claim: Control WT animals were C57BL/6 J mice from The Jackson Laboratory.
source: Control WT animals were C57BL/6 J mice from The Jackson Laboratory (Jax #000664).
evidence: This describes the control animals used.

claim: Both male and female mice (> 6 weeks) were used for all experiments.
source: Both male and female (> 6  weeks) mice were used for all experiments, and the number of mice of each sex used to generate each dataset is reported in the legend.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The experimenter was blinded to genotype throughout the experiments.
source: The experimenter was blinded to genotype throughout.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to reduce bias.

claim: Substance P-sniffer cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of Substance P (EC50=21 nM).
source: These cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of Substance P (EC50=21 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but were insensitive to CGRPα.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Substance P-sniffer cells were insensitive to CGRPα.
source: These cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of Substance P (EC50=21 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but were insensitive to CGRPα.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CGRP-sniffer cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of CGRPα (EC50=27 nM).
source: These cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of CGRPα (EC50=27 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but were insensitive to Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CGRP-sniffer cells were insensitive to Substance P.
source: These cells responded to low nanomolar concentrations of CGRPα (EC50=27 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but were insensitive to Substance P.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DKO mice scratched robustly following intradermal chloroquine injection, a response indistinguishable from WT animals.
source: DKO mice scratched robustly following intradermal chloroquine injection, a response indistinguishable from WT animals (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Acetic acid injection evoked comparable writhing behavior in both WT and DKO mice.
source: First, we dosed mice with acetic acid via intraperitoneal injection. This evoked comparable writhing behavior in both WT and DKO mice (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Pairing saccharin with LiCl injection elicited a strong and indistinguishable conditioned taste aversion in both WT and DKO mice.
source: Notably, pairing saccharin with LiCl injection elicited a strong and indistinguishable conditioned taste aversion in both WT and DKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NKR1 antagonists are effective anti-emetics.
source: Next, because NKR1 antagonists are effective anti-emetics, we wondered whether the two peptides contribute to nausea-like behavior in mice (Warr et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous clinical studies.

claim: NKR1 antagonists have been proposed to treat itch.
source: NKR1 antagonists have also been proposed to treat itch (Pojawa-Gołąb et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Oxaliplatin-induced cold allodynia is known to depend, in part, on CGRPα-positive silent cold-sensing neurons.
source: Second, we treated mice with the chemotherapeutic drug oxaliplatin which evokes extreme cold allodynia that is known to depend, in part, on CGRPα-positive silent cold-sensing neurons (MacDonald et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lithium chloride induces gastrointestinal malaise in many species.
source: In many species, lithium chloride induces gastrointestinal malaise and when paired with a normally attractive tastant produces a marked conditioned taste aversion (Garcia et al., 1955).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a classic study.

claim: The CGRP receptor consists of two co-receptors encoded by the genes Calcrl and Ramp1.
source: The CGRP receptor consists of two co-receptors encoded by the genes Calcrl and Ramp1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CGRP receptor structure.

claim: Calca deletion largely abolished endogenous CGRPα signaling.
source: Thus, Calca deletion largely abolished endogenous CGRPα signaling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the CGRP-sniffer cell data in Figure 1F-H.
